newsitem.title: FRANCE: Bikkembergs gazes at navel, Marechal sees junkies.
newsitem.headline: Bikkembergs gazes at navel, Marechal sees junkies.

text.p: Belgium's Dirk Bikkembergs sent out an understated winter ready-to-wear collection for the unobtrusive woman, while Swiss designer Bertrand Marechal drew his inspiration from strung-out suburban drug addicts.
Bikkembergs' show on Monday night was a marathon of dark, asymetrically cut jackets over slacks, whose waistlines sloped under the navel, giving supermodels' bellies a few extra ounces.
A detail occasionally emerged from the blur: a braid down the arm of a navy blue sweater, the silver flash of a ruffled shirt under an austere jacket or the gleaming knot of a necktie.
From a man who regularly attracts a mad crush of admirers at his late night events, it was an exercise in navel-gazing aimed at women who would rather blend than stand out in a crowd.
Three blue stripes at the bottom of an olive knit tank top 15 minutes into the show sent critics scribbling madly. Another 10 and a glimpse of white gleamed from a pair of print dresses.
Relief came in a handful of sombre evening gowns with glistening belts that curlicued down the front, or in back.

Meanwhile, where Marechal's show was short on substance, he made up for it with fun: a model flung open her white fur coat to reveal her naked as the day she was born, sheer patchwork slip dresses bared plenty of flesh, and bracelets and chokers were etched on the skin with felt-tipped pen.
The collection, which Marechal said was inspired by junkies in Paris' depressed suburbs, was often a a bit ragged around the edges and uneven at the seams.
But such imperfections are understandable from a man who sews all of his designs at home on his sewing machine and stages his fashion shows at home or in a flat on loan from a friend.

Earlier, France's living fashion legend Yves Saint-Laurent shunned the crowds and crush of the catwalk, kicking off the season with a sample 31 outfits presented to a tiny audience of about 20 reporters in his plush couture salon.
Flamboyant swan feather coats, flashy three-tone jersey dresses, and a gold lame dinner tunic aside, Saint-Laurent's razor-edge tailoring and cool elegance had a minimalist flavour.
It showed in the starkness of a sleeveless black satin slipdress, austere black coats on skinny trousers or transparent tee-shirts and slacks of stretchy onion-skin jersey.

Saint-Laurent's feisty president Pierre Berge shrugged off suggestions that Paris was losing its grip as fashion capital as British upstarts grab the headlines and business-minded Italians and Americans outsell their French rivals.

"People are confusing creation and marketing. The kings of marketing are in Milan, with Gucci and Prada, or in New York, with Calvin Klein and Donna Karan. But the creativity is still in France," he said.

To prove Saint Laurent's superiority over the likes of Britain's John Galliano, whose debut collection for former Saint Laurent employer Christian Dior was the triumph of January's couture shows, Berge said Saint Laurent had tripled his haute couture sales in the year to January 1997.

Last month, Saint Laurent created a stir when he told the German magazine Focus that collections by Galliano and fellow Briton Alexander McQueen, Givenchy's new designer, were "ridiculous spectacles which would have been more in keeping with a rock concert. I was totally bored with their shows."
